procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Registrar of the Supreme Court returning the petitioner's petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a Civil Miscellaneous Petition No. 915 of 1957 under Article 71(1) of the Constitution, challenging the election to the office of the President. The Registrar returned the petition for not complying with the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 (Act XXXI of 1952) and Order XXXVII-A of the Supreme Court Rules. The petitioner then appealed the Registrar's order to the Supreme Court.

decision.appeal_result: This appeal is dismissed. Petition dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a petition founded upon doubts as to the validity of the Presidential election is not covered by the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, or the Supreme Court Rules.

facts: A petitioner, describing himself as an intending candidate, filed a petition in the Supreme Court challenging the validity of the Presidential election.
The petitioner argued that his petition was founded on 'doubts' about the election's validity, not a 'dispute'.
He contended that because it was about 'doubts', it was not covered by the procedural requirements of the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, or the Supreme Court Rules.
law: Article 71(1) of the Constitution gives the Supreme Court jurisdiction to inquire into and decide all 'doubts and disputes' arising from a Presidential election.
The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, and the Supreme Court Rules (O. XXXVII-A) set out the specific procedures and conditions for bringing such a challenge to the Court.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's attempt to distinguish between a 'doubt' and a 'dispute'.
The Court reasoned that once an election has been held, any 'doubt' concerning its validity is a material basis for challenging it.
It held that the word 'dispute' is broad enough to include a 'doubt'.
The Court noted that the petitioner's own prayer—to have the election quashed—showed that the petition was, in substance, one 'calling the election in question'.
Therefore, the petition must satisfy the requirements laid out in the Act and the Court's Rules.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, concluding that a petition founded on 'doubts' about an election's validity is essentially a 'dispute' that calls the election into question. As such, it is covered by and must comply with the procedural requirements of the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, and the relevant Supreme Court Rules.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, and the relevant Supreme Court Rules are void because they derogate from the jurisdiction conferred on the Supreme Court under Article 71(1) of the Constitution.

facts: A petitioner, an intending candidate in the Presidential election, filed a petition in the Supreme Court under Article 71(1) of the Constitution to challenge the election's validity.
The Court's Registrar returned the petition because it did not comply with the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, and the relevant Supreme Court Rules.

The petitioner appealed, arguing that the Act and the Rules were void because they unconstitutionally restricted the Supreme Court's broad jurisdiction under Article 71(1) to inquire into all doubts and disputes related to the election.

law.description: This article merely prescribes the forum—the Supreme Court—where doubts and disputes concerning the election of the President and Vice-President will be heard.
This article explicitly authorizes Parliament to make laws for regulating any matter relating to or connected with the election of the President or Vice-President.

The right to stand for election and the right to challenge an election are not common law rights. They are statutory rights that must be conferred by a specific law and can only be enforced according to the conditions laid down in that law.

application: The Supreme Court reasoned that Article 71(1) only establishes *where* an election dispute is to be decided (the Supreme Court), but not *how* or under what conditions a petition can be brought.
The Court found that the 'how' is determined by Parliament, acting under the authority granted to it by Article 71(3).
The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, was passed by Parliament in accordance with this constitutional authority.
Therefore, the Act and the associated Rules do not derogate from the Court's jurisdiction; rather, they regulate the procedure for invoking that jurisdiction.
A person wishing to challenge an election has no rights apart from those given by the statute and must follow the procedures and conditions it lays out.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, and the Supreme Court Rules are constitutionally valid. They do not derogate from the Court's jurisdiction under Article 71(1) because they are procedural laws properly enacted by Parliament under the authority of Article 71(3) to regulate how election disputes are brought before the Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether a citizen has a right to approach the Supreme Court for relief whenever an election has been held in breach of constitutional provisions, independent of the conditions laid down in the statute.

facts: A petitioner, describing himself as an intending candidate, filed a petition in the Supreme Court to challenge the validity of the Presidential election.

The petitioner argued that as a citizen, he had a right to approach the Supreme Court for relief whenever an election was held in breach of constitutional provisions, regardless of the rules set out in any specific law.
law: Article 71(1) of the Constitution designates the Supreme Court as the forum for inquiring into disputes related to the election of the President and Vice-President.
Article 71(3) of the Constitution authorizes Parliament to make laws to regulate any matter relating to or connected with such elections.
The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 (Act XXXI of 1952) is the law passed by Parliament under the authority of Article 71(3).
The right to stand for election and the right to move for setting aside an election are not common law rights; they must be conferred by statute.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that while Article 71(1) establishes the Court as the correct forum, it does not grant an independent right to challenge an election.

The actual right to challenge an election and the specific procedure for doing so are governed by the statute created by Parliament, which is the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.
The Court held that this Act was validly passed under the authority of Article 71(3).
Therefore, any person wishing to challenge an election must strictly follow the conditions and procedures laid down in that Act.
A citizen does not have a separate or independent right to challenge an election outside the framework of the statute.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, concluding that the right of a person to file an application to set aside an election is determined exclusively by the statute passed by Parliament (the Act of 1952). A citizen has no rights to challenge an election apart from those specifically granted by that statute.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a petition founded upon doubts as to the validity of the Presidential election is not covered by the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, or the Supreme Court Rules.
appellant_arguments: The petition is outside the purview of the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, and the Supreme Court Rules (O. XXXVII-A).

The Act and Rules apply only when there is a 'dispute', whereas the petition is founded upon 'doubts' concerning the election, which the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to inquire into under the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: A petition raising 'doubts' about the validity of an election is, in substance, a petition calling the election into question and is therefore a 'dispute' covered by the Act and the Rules.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, and the relevant Supreme Court Rules are void because they derogate from the jurisdiction conferred on the Supreme Court under Article 71(1) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The Act and Rules, by imposing procedural and financial conditions (like who can file, court fees, and security deposits), improperly limit the broad jurisdiction granted to the Supreme Court by Article 71(1) to decide all doubts and disputes.
respondent_arguments: The Act and Rules are valid as they are enacted by Parliament under the authority of Article 71(3) of the Constitution, which explicitly allows Parliament to regulate matters relating to the election.
Article 71(1) only establishes the Supreme Court as the forum for disputes, while the right to move the court and the procedure for doing so are properly determined by the statute.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a citizen has a right to approach the Supreme Court for relief whenever an election has been held in breach of constitutional provisions, independent of the conditions laid down in the statute.
appellant_arguments: A citizen has an inherent right to approach the Supreme Court under Article 71(1) whenever a Presidential election has been held in breach of constitutional provisions, regardless of the limitations in the statute.
respondent_arguments: The right to file an application to set aside an election is not an inherent right but is determined solely by the statute that creates it (the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952).
A petitioner has no rights apart from the statute and must strictly bring themselves within its provisions to challenge an election.

statutes.act_name: Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 (Act XXXI of 1952)

cases.case_name: N. B. Khare v. The Election Commission of India
cases.citation: This is the case being decided; no prior cases were cited.
cases.principle: The right to stand for election and the right to move for setting aside an election are not common law rights but are statutory rights. They must be conferred by statute and can only be enforced in accordance with the conditions laid down in that statute.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The right to stand for election and the right to move for setting aside an election are not common law rights; they are conferred by statute and can only be enforced in accordance with the conditions laid down therein. Article 71(1) of the Constitution merely prescribes the forum for election disputes, while the right to move the court and the procedure for it are determined by the Act of Parliament as authorized by Article 71(3). A petitioner has no rights apart from those given by the statute and must strictly bring themselves within its provisions.
obiter: Although there can be no rigid and inexorable convention that a wage structure once fixed can never be changed to the prejudice of the workmen, the wages of workmen cannot be allowed to fall below the bare subsistence level.
No industry can have the right to exist if it cannot be maintained except by bringing the wages below the bare subsistence level.
The Constitution of India seeks to create a democratic welfare state and secure social and economic justice to the citizens.

Growth of industries and the advent of collective bargaining between organized labour and capital with consequent industrial legislation have made absolute freedom of contract and the-doctrine of laissez faire things of the past and they have now to yield place to principles of social welfare and common good.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The right to challenge a Presidential election is not a common law right but is a right created and governed entirely by statute. The Constitution, in Article 71(1), merely prescribes the Supreme Court as the exclusive forum for such challenges, while Article 71(3) explicitly empowers Parliament to regulate all matters relating to the election, including who can file a petition and under what conditions. Therefore, a petitioner has no rights apart from those conferred by the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, and must strictly bring themselves within the four corners of that statute to have their petition heard.
legal_tests_applied: The right to stand for election and the right to move for setting aside an election are not common law rights; they must be conferred by statute and can be enforced only in accordance with the conditions laid down therein.

A constitutional provision establishing a court's jurisdiction (Article 71(1)) must be read in conjunction with other provisions that grant Parliament the power to regulate matters related to that jurisdiction (Article 71(3)).
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the distinction between a petition based on 'doubts' and one raising a 'dispute', finding that a petition founded on the allegation that there are doubts as to the validity of an election is, in substance, a petition calling the election in question and is therefore governed by the Act and the Rules.

The argument that the Act and Rules derogate from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 71(1) failed because the court held that Article 71(1) merely prescribes the forum, while Article 71(3) explicitly authorizes Parliament to regulate the conditions for presenting an election petition.

The claim of an inherent right for any citizen to challenge an election was dismissed because the right to file an application for setting aside an election must be determined by the statute which gives it, and the petitioner has no rights apart from that statute.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that a petition raising 'doubts' about an election's validity is substantively a 'dispute' covered by the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.
The court affirmed that the Act and Rules are valid exercises of Parliament's authority under Article 71(3) of the Constitution to regulate matters relating to the Presidential election.
The court endorsed the principle that the right to challenge an election is purely a creature of statute, and a petitioner must strictly comply with the provisions of that statute to have standing.
